In [[algebra]], a [[multivariate polynomial]]
: <math>f(x)=\sum_\alpha a_\alpha x^\alpha\text{, where }\alpha=(i_1,\dots,i_r)\in \mathbb{N}^r \text{, and } x^\alpha=x_1^{i_1} \cdots x_r^{i_r},</math> 
is '''quasi-homogeneous''' or '''weighted homogeneous''', if there exist ''r'' integers <math>w_1, \ldots, w_r</math>, called '''weights''' of the variables, such that the sum <math>w=w_1i_1+ \cdots + w_ri_r</math> is the same for all nonzero terms of {{math|''f''}}. This sum {{math|''w''}} is the ''weight'' or the ''degree'' of the polynomial.

The term ''quasi-homogeneous'' comes from the fact that a polynomial {{math|''f''}} is quasi-homogeneous if and only if
:<math> f(\lambda^{w_1} x_1, \ldots, \lambda^{w_r} x_r)=\lambda^w f(x_1,\ldots, x_r)</math> 
for every <math>\lambda</math> in any [[field (mathematics)|field]] containing the coefficients.

A polynomial <math>f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)</math> is quasi-homogeneous with weights <math>w_1, \ldots, w_r</math> if and only if 
:<math>f(y_1^{w_1}, \ldots, y_n^{w_n})</math> 
is a [[homogeneous polynomial]] in the <math>y_i</math>.  In particular, a homogeneous polynomial is always quasi-homogeneous, with all weights equal to 1.

A polynomial is quasi-homogeneous if and only if all the <math>\alpha</math> belong to the same [[affine hyperplane]]. As the [[Newton polygon|Newton polytope]] of the polynomial is the [[convex hull]] of the set <math>\{\alpha \mid a_\alpha \neq0 \},</math> the quasi-homogeneous polynomials may also be defined as the polynomials that have a degenerate Newton polytope (here "degenerate" means "contained in some affine hyperplane").

==Introduction==
Consider the polynomial <math>f(x,y)=5x^3y^3+xy^9-2y^{12}</math>, which is not homogeneous. However, if instead of considering <math>f(\lambda x, \lambda y)</math> we use the pair <math>(\lambda^3, \lambda)</math> to test homogeneity, then

:<math>f(\lambda^3 x, \lambda y) = 5(\lambda^3x)^3(\lambda y)^3 + (\lambda^3x)(\lambda y)^9 - 2(\lambda y)^{12} = \lambda^{12}f(x,y).</math>

We say that <math>f(x,y)</math> is a quasi-homogeneous polynomial of '''type'''
{{math|(3,1)}}, because its three pairs {{math|(''i''<sub>1</sub>, ''i''<sub>2</sub>)}} of exponents {{math|(3,3)}}, {{math|(1,9)}} and {{math|(0,12)}} all satisfy the linear equation <math>3i_1+1i_2=12</math>. In particular, this says that the Newton polytope of <math>f(x,y)</math> lies in the affine space with equation <math>3x+y = 12</math> inside <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math>.

The above equation is equivalent to this new one: <math>\tfrac{1}{4}x + \tfrac{1}{12}y = 1</math>. Some authors<ref>{{cite journal |first=J. |last=Steenbrink |title=Intersection form for quasi-homogeneous singularities  |journal=Compositio Mathematica |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=211–223 See p. 211 |year=1977 |issn=0010-437X |url=http://archive.numdam.org/article/CM_1977__34_2_211_0.pdf}}</ref> prefer to use this last condition and prefer to say that our polynomial is quasi-homogeneous of type <math>(\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{12})</math>.

As noted above, a homogeneous polynomial <math>g(x,y)</math> of degree {{math|''d''}} is just a quasi-homogeneous polynomial of type {{math|(1,1)}}; in this case all its pairs of exponents will satisfy the equation <math>1i_1+1i_2 = d</math>.

==Definition==
Let <math>f(x)</math> be a polynomial in {{math|''r''}} variables <math>x=x_1\ldots x_r</math> with coefficients in a [[commutative ring]] {{math|''R''}}. We express it as a finite sum

: <math>f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^r} a_\alpha x^\alpha, \alpha=(i_1,\ldots,i_r), a_\alpha\in \mathbb{R}.</math>

We say that {{math|''f''}} is '''quasi-homogeneous of type''' <math>\varphi=(\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_r)</math>, <math>\varphi_i\in\mathbb{N}</math>, if there exists some <math>a \in \mathbb{R}</math> such that

: <math>\langle \alpha,\varphi \rangle = \sum_k^ri_k\varphi_k = a</math>

whenever <math>a_\alpha\neq 0</math>.
